title: Food, drinks and ordering
objectives: I can order food and drinks politely in a padaria, a lanchonete and a restaurant.
I can say what I like, what I want and what I prefer.
I can use the present tense of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
I can ask for more, less or a little of something.
I can talk about meals and ask for the bill.

vocabulary.note: The Brazilian word for menu. In Portugal people say ementa.
Feminine: a garçonete. To get the waiter's attention say com licença or moço, moça.
More than a bakery. A padaria also serves coffee, sandwiches and breakfast at a counter, and sells basic groceries.
A casual place with sandwiches, snacks, juices and coffee.
At a restaurante por quilo you serve yourself from a buffet, put your plate on a scale and pay for the weight.

dialogues.title: Breakfast at the padaria
dialogues.context: Ricardo stops at a padaria on his way to work and orders breakfast at the counter.

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.pt: Bom dia! Pois não?
lines.en: Good morning! How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Ricardo
lines.pt: Bom dia! Eu queria um pão na chapa e um café com leite, por favor.
lines.en: Good morning! I would like a buttered toasted roll and a coffee with milk, please.

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.pt: Só isso?
lines.en: Is that all?

lines.speaker: Ricardo
lines.pt: Me vê também um pão de queijo.
lines.en: Give me a cheese bread as well.

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.pt: Tá bom. Mais alguma coisa?
lines.en: Okay. Anything else?

lines.speaker: Ricardo
lines.pt: Só isso. Ah, o café é sem açúcar, por favor.
lines.en: That is all. Oh, the coffee is without sugar, please.

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.pt: Um pão na chapa, um café com leite sem açúcar e um pão de queijo. Tudo certo?
lines.en: A buttered toasted roll, a coffee with milk without sugar and a cheese bread. All right?

lines.speaker: Ricardo
lines.pt: Tudo certo! Obrigado.
lines.en: All right! Thank you.

lines.speaker: Simone
lines.pt: Bom apetite!
lines.en: Enjoy your meal!

lines.speaker: Ricardo
lines.pt: Obrigado! Até amanhã!
lines.en: Thank you! See you tomorrow!

dialogues.title: Lunch at a restaurante por quilo
dialogues.context: Camila and André have lunch together at a restaurant where you pay by the weight of your plate.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: André, você gosta de feijão?
lines.en: André, do you like beans?

lines.speaker: André
lines.pt: Gosto, sim! Eu como arroz e feijão todo dia.
lines.en: Yes, I do! I eat rice and beans every day.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: E você prefere carne ou frango?
lines.en: And do you prefer beef or chicken?

lines.speaker: André
lines.pt: Prefiro frango. Eu não como carne.
lines.en: I prefer chicken. I do not eat beef.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Você quer salada?
lines.en: Do you want salad?

lines.speaker: André
lines.pt: Quero um pouco de salada e mais arroz.
lines.en: I want a little salad and more rice.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: E para beber? Você quer suco?
lines.en: And to drink? Do you want juice?

lines.speaker: André
lines.pt: Quero, sim. Suco de laranja. E você?
lines.en: Yes, I do. Orange juice. And you?

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Eu prefiro água.
lines.en: I prefer water.

lines.speaker: André
lines.pt: Este restaurante por quilo é muito bom!
lines.en: This by-the-kilo restaurant is very good!

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: É, e a conta não é cara.
lines.en: Yes, and the bill is not expensive.

dialogues.title: Dinner at a restaurant
dialogues.context: Clara and her brother Tiago have dinner at a restaurant. Paulo is their waiter.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Boa noite! Aqui está o cardápio.
lines.en: Good evening! Here is the menu.

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.pt: Obrigada. Tiago, o que você quer?
lines.en: Thank you. Tiago, what do you want?

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.pt: Eu queria o prato feito com frango. E você?
lines.en: I would like the set plate with chicken. And you?

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.pt: Eu prefiro peixe com arroz e salada.
lines.en: I prefer fish with rice and salad.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Muito bem. O que vocês querem beber?
lines.en: Very good. What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.pt: Eu quero uma cerveja.
lines.en: I want a beer.

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.pt: Eu queria um suco de laranja, por favor. Sem açúcar.
lines.en: I would like an orange juice, please. Without sugar.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Certo. Mais alguma coisa?
lines.en: Right. Anything else?

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.pt: Só isso, obrigado.
lines.en: That is all, thank you.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Claro. Um minuto, por favor.
lines.en: Of course. One minute, please.

grammar.title: The regular present tense: -ar, -er and -ir verbs
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir in the infinitive, the form you find in a dictionary. To conjugate a regular verb in the present, remove the ending to get the stem and add the endings for the subject. Falar (to speak) has the stem fal-, comer (to eat) has com- and abrir (to open) has abr-.

In the eu form all three groups end in -o: falo, como, abro. In the nós form the endings are -amos, -emos and -imos: falamos, comemos, abrimos. For você, ele, ela and a gente the endings are -a for -ar verbs and -e for -er and -ir verbs: fala, come, abre. For vocês, eles and elas the ending is -am for -ar verbs and -em for -er and -ir verbs: falam, comem, abrem. The nasal endings -am and -em sound like the nasal diphthongs in são and têm, and the stress stays on the same syllable as in the singular: FA-la, FA-lam.

The pronoun is often dropped because the ending identifies the subject: Como arroz todo dia. Keep it when you need emphasis or when the verb form alone would be unclear, as with fala, which can mean you, he or she speak.

The present tense describes habits and facts (Eu como arroz e feijão) and general truths. Brazilians also use a separate progressive form for what is happening right now, which you will learn later. To make a negative, place não before the verb: Eu não bebo cerveja.

grammar.title: Querer, gostar de, preferir and eu queria
grammar.explanation:
Querer, to want, is irregular in two forms: eu quero and você quer. The other forms are regular: nós queremos, vocês querem. Preferir, to prefer, is regular in its endings: eu prefiro, você prefere, nós preferimos, vocês preferem. Gostar, to like, is regular but always needs de after it: Eu gosto de café, Ela gosta de feijão. The same de joins with articles, so you say gosto do pão de queijo and gosto da salada. After gostar de you can also use a verb in the infinitive: Gosto de comer peixe.

For polite requests, Brazilians use eu queria, which literally means I wanted but works like the English I would like. It is softer than eu quero. Eu queria um café, por favor is the standard way to order. Eu quero um café is not rude, especially when you add por favor, and it is heard often in casual places, but queria is a safer choice with people you do not know.

In a padaria, a lanchonete or at a counter you will often hear me vê. Me vê um pão de queijo literally means see a cheese bread for me and is a friendly, informal way of saying give me a cheese bread. Staff say Pois não? or Pois não, pode falar to ask what you want. The phrase Mais alguma coisa? means anything else? and Só isso? means is that all?

grammar.title: Questions and short answers
grammar.explanation:
A yes or no question in Portuguese has the same word order as a statement, and the difference is intonation: your voice rises at the end. Você gosta de feijão? is literally you like beans? There is no word like do or does. You can also add né at the end of a statement to ask for confirmation, like right or isn't it: A aula é às dez, né?

The normal way to answer yes or no is to repeat the verb. Você quer um cafezinho? Quero. Você gosta de peixe? Gosto. For emphasis add sim: Quero, sim. To say no, use não in front of the verb, and often say não twice: Não, não gosto. In polite refusals you can say Não, obrigado or Não, obrigada.

An or question offers a choice: Você prefere carne ou frango? Answer with the verb or the item: Prefiro frango. Question words from unit 3 are used in the same way: O que você quer? Onde é o restaurante? Quem paga a conta? A useful phrase when ordering is para beber, meaning to drink: E para beber?

When you hear a question with a verb, pay attention to the ending, because it tells you who is being asked. Você quer suco? Vocês querem suco? The subject can be omitted in the answer, as in Queremos.

examples.en: Do you want a small coffee?
Do you prefer beef or chicken?

grammar.title: Quantities: um pouco de, mais, menos, com and sem
grammar.explanation:
Um pouco de means a little. It is followed by a noun and does not change: um pouco de arroz, um pouco de açúcar. Mais means more and menos means less or fewer. They never change for gender or number and go directly before the noun: mais arroz, menos açúcar, mais pães. To say one more, use mais um or mais uma, agreeing with the thing: mais um café, mais uma cerveja.

Com means with and sem means without. They work the same way in English: café com leite, café sem açúcar, pão com manteiga. A short request with sem or com sounds completely natural: Um suco sem açúcar, por favor.

The word só means only or just, and so Só a conta, por favor means just the bill, please. In a padaria you will often hear Só isso?, which means is that all?

To talk about meals, use the article: o café da manhã, o almoço and o jantar. Brazilians usually have a light breakfast, a main lunch and a lighter dinner, and a small snack in the afternoon called lanche da tarde. To say what you have for a meal, use comer: Eu como pão no café da manhã.

examples.pt: Mais um café com leite, por favor.
examples.en: One more coffee with milk, please.

examples.pt: Um suco sem açúcar, por favor.

culture.title: Eating and drinking in Brazil
culture.text:
The Brazilian day is organized around three meals. Breakfast, o café da manhã, is light: coffee with milk, bread with butter or cheese, pão na chapa, often a piece of fruit, and on weekends pão de queijo. Lunch, o almoço, is the main meal and usually eaten around noon or one. Many Brazilians eat arroz e feijão every day, with meat or chicken, a salad and something fried or baked. Dinner is lighter and sometimes just a sandwich or a soup.

For a quick, cheap lunch, many people go to a restaurante por quilo, where you fill your plate from a buffet and pay for its weight, or order a prato feito, abbreviated to PF, which gives you a complete plate at a fixed price. In a padaria you can have coffee and bread at the counter at any time of day, and in a lanchonete you order juices, sandwiches and snacks like pastel, coxinha and pão de queijo.

Coffee is everywhere. A cafezinho is offered in offices, shops and homes, and refusing is possible but a little unusual. Popular drinks include fresh suco, guaraná, which is a sweet soft drink made from an Amazonian fruit, and água de coco. In restaurants a service charge of about ten percent is usually added to the bill. To ask for the bill, say A conta, por favor, or catch the waiter's eye and make a writing gesture in the air. Before eating, people say bom apetite, and for a toast they say saúde.
